- library-skills: Use Library Skills to discover, install, refresh, repair, check, and manage agent skills from installed packages.
- typer: Typer best practices and conventions. Use when working with Typer CLIs. Keeps Typer code clean and up to date with the latest features and patterns, updated with new versions. Write new code or refactor and update old code.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). # Detection rule configuration.
#
# Loaded by settings.py::load_settings() and turned into Rule instances via
# engine.build_rules(). This is a transcription of the baseline previously
# hardcoded in engine/rules.py::default_rules() (see docs/rule-config-plan.md).
#
# Each rule: {id, type, enabled?, severity?, params}.
#   - type "threshold": stateful per-IP sliding window (brute force, scanning).
#     params: match, threshold, window_seconds, distinct_by?, title?,
#     description?, max_evidence? (default 20).
#   - type "signature": stateless per-line regex matching (SQLi, traversal, ...).
#     params: target, patterns, title?, description?, case_sensitive?
#     (default false), min_hits? (default 1), max_evidence? (default 20),
#     max_decode_passes? (default 2 — nested URL-decode attempts tried
#     against each value before giving up on evasion via encoding).
# Supplying a rule with an existing id overrides it; enabled: false disables it;
# a new id adds a rule. See docs/engine-plan.md §6.1.
#
# `engine` and `correlation` are both optional; omitting either (or the whole
# section) falls back to the defaults shown below.

# Engine-wide behavior (engine/engine.py::Engine), independent of any one rule.
engine:
  # Ceiling on stored evidence lines per finding, applied after collection.
  # A rule's own `max_evidence` param (if lower) already wins during
  # collection; this only trims further.
  max_evidence: 20

# Cross-rule correlation (engine/correlation.py::Correlator): how findings
# for the same IP are clustered into incidents.
correlation:
  # Findings within this many minutes of each other (by the running cluster
  # span) are grouped into one incident.
  window_minutes: 10

# default shown below.
reporting:
  # Directory that generated `report_YYYY_MM_DD_HH_MM_SS.html` files are
  # written to. A relative path is resolved against the current working
  # directory; the directory is created automatically if it does not exist.
  output_dir: reports

      patterns:
        - "union\\s+select"
        - "\\bor\\s+1\\s*=\\s*1\\b"
        - "'\\s*or\\s*'1'\\s*=\\s*'1"
        - '"\s*or\s*"1"\s*=\s*"1'
        - "'\\s*or\\s+\\w"

        - "'\\s*#"

1	# trace-log-sec
2	
3	A security log analysis CLI that parses webserver and authentication logs, detects suspicious activity with configurable rules, and correlates related findings into incidents.
4	
5	It processes NCSA Combined access logs and BSD syslog auth logs, runs signature and threshold detectors, groups multi-signal activity by IP into correlated incidents, and writes both a terminal summary and a standalone HTML report.
6	
7	---
8	
9	## Requirements
10	
11	- **Python** 3.12 or 3.13
12	- **[uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/)** (recommended) — installs the project and its dependencies from the lockfile
13	
14	---
15	
16	## Installation
17	
18	Clone the repository and install into a local virtual environment:
19	
20	```bash
21	git clone https://github.com/Kenndal/trace-log-sec.git
22	cd trace-log-sec
23	uv sync
24	```
25	
26	That creates `.venv/`, editable-installs the package, and registers the `trace-log-sec` console script.
27	
28	To include the test tooling as well:
29	
30	```bash
31	uv sync --group test
32	```
33	
34	For linting / typing / pre-commit hooks:
35	
36	```bash
37	uv sync --group dev --group test
38	```
39	
40	Verify the install:
41	
42	```bash
43	uv run trace-log-sec --help
44	```
45	
46	### Alternative: pip
47	
48	If you prefer pip over uv (still requires Python ≥ 3.12):
49	
50	```bash
51	python -m venv .venv
52	source .venv/bin/activate   # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
53	pip install -e .
54	trace-log-sec --help
55	```
56	
57	---
58	
59	## CLI usage
60	
61	The tool exposes two commands: `analyze` and `list-reports`.
62	
63	```bash
64	uv run trace-log-sec --help
65	uv run trace-log-sec analyze --help
66	uv run trace-log-sec list-reports --help
67	```
68	
69	### Analyze logs
70	
71	```bash
72	uv run trace-log-sec analyze AUTH.log WEBSERVER.log
73	```
74	
75	`analyze` accepts one or more `*.log` files as positional arguments. Format — NCSA Combined access log vs BSD syslog auth log — is **auto-detected per file** from content (first parseable non-blank line within the first 20 lines), so files can be given in any order or mix. The shipped default rule set (`config.yaml` at the repo root) is used, and findings are correlated across files by source IP.
76	
77	Quick start against the bundled sample logs:
78	
79	```bash
80	uv run trace-log-sec analyze \
81	  samples/auth_incidents.log \
82	  samples/webserver_incidents.log
83	```
84	
85	#### Options
86	
87	| Option | Overrides | Default |
88	|---|---|---|
89	| `--max-evidence N` | `engine.max_evidence` | from `config.yaml` (built-in default: `20`) |
90	| `--window-minutes N` | `correlation.window_minutes` | from `config.yaml` (built-in default: `10`) |
91	| `--reference-time DATETIME` | syslog year anchor | newest web-log timestamp in this run, else current UTC time |
92	| `--config PATH` | the entire config file (rules included) | bundled `config.yaml` at the repo root |
93	
94	Precedence is always **command-line flag → `config.yaml` → built-in default**: an option only takes effect if explicitly passed.
95	
96	```bash
97	uv run trace-log-sec analyze \
98	  --max-evidence 5 \
99	  --window-minutes 30 \
100	  --reference-time 2025-11-12T12:00:00 \
101	  auth.log webserver.log
102	```
103	
104	`--reference-time` accepts `%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S`, `%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S`, or `%Y-%m-%d`.
105	
106	Use `--config` to swap out the whole config file — rules, `engine`, `correlation`, and `reporting` sections — for a single run, without touching the bundled `config.yaml`:
107	
108	```bash
109	uv run trace-log-sec analyze --config custom-config.yaml auth.log webserver.log
110	```
111	
112	`--config` must point to an existing, readable file; `--max-evidence`/`--window-minutes` still override whatever that file (or its defaults) sets. `list-reports` also accepts `--config`, so a run's HTML reports can be listed from the same custom `reporting.output_dir`.
113	
114	#### Input validation
115	
116	Before analysis starts, every path is checked. Problems are collected and reported together:
117	
118	- file must exist and be a regular file
119	- extension must be `.log`
120	- paths must be unique (duplicates rejected)
121	- at least one file is required
122	
123	Unrecognized formats are skipped with a warning (non-fatal), unless *every* given file is unrecognized — that is treated as an error.
124	
125	#### Auth-log year anchoring
126	
127	BSD syslog lines have **no year**. The CLI resolves the year as follows:
128	
129	1. Explicit `--reference-time` if passed
130	2. Else the newest Combined-log timestamp among web logs in this run (read cheaply from each file’s tail)
131	3. Else the current UTC time — and a warning is printed, because archived auth-only logs can get the wrong year (which silently skews threshold windows and correlation)
132	
133	When analyzing both web and auth logs together, you usually do **not** need `--reference-time`. Pass it for historical auth-only runs.
134	
135	#### Terminal output
136	
137	```
138	=== FINDINGS ===
139	  [HIGH    ] ssh_brute_force        ip=198.51.100.23  count=8   SSH Brute Force
140	  ...
141	
142	=== INCIDENTS ===
143	  INC-a1b2c3d4e5 [HIGH] 203.0.113.150
144	    ...narrative...
145	
146	=== PARSE ERRORS ===
147	  (none)
148	
149	=== STATS === lines_read=4167 parsed=4160 malformed=7 findings=12 incidents=3 (0.0421s)
150	
151	HTML report written to reports/report_2026_07_31_12_00_00.html
152	```
153	
154	Findings are sorted by severity (highest first), then rule id. Parse errors show source, line number, reason, and a raw snippet.
155	
156	#### HTML report
157	
158	Every successful `analyze` also writes a standalone HTML report under the directory configured in `config.yaml` (`reporting.output_dir`, default `reports/`). The directory is created automatically if missing. Filename format:
159	
160	```
161	report_YYYY_MM_DD_HH_MM_SS.html
162	```
163	
164	Relative paths resolve against the **current working directory**. A write failure (e.g. unwritable directory) only warns — the terminal analysis is never discarded.
165	
166	The HTML report includes:
167	
168	- executive summary tiles (findings, incidents, lines read/parsed/malformed, duration)
169	- correlated incident cards with nested findings and expandable evidence
170	- findings table (severity, IP, count, sources, time span, description, evidence)
171	- parse-error table when any malformed lines were seen
172	
173	All log-derived values are HTML-escaped before embedding (attacker-controlled content must not become stored XSS when the report is opened in a browser).
174	
175	### List previous reports
176	
177	```bash
178	uv run trace-log-sec list-reports
179	```
180	
181	Scans `reporting.output_dir` and prints generated reports newest-first with their timestamps. Files that do not match the `report_YYYY_MM_DD_HH_MM_SS.html` naming convention are ignored. A missing directory yields an empty result, not an error.
182	
183	Accepts `--config PATH` as well, to list reports from a custom config's `reporting.output_dir` instead of the bundled `config.yaml`'s.
184	
185	---
186	
187	## Configuration
188	
189	All runtime knobs live in `config.yaml` at the repo root (shipped with the package):
190	
191	```yaml
192	engine:
193	  max_evidence: 20          # ceiling on evidence lines stored per finding
194	
195	correlation:
196	  window_minutes: 10        # IP clustering window for incidents
197	
198	reporting:
199	  output_dir: reports       # HTML report directory (cwd-relative or absolute)
200	
201	rules:
202	  - id: ssh_brute_force
203	    type: threshold
204	    severity: high
205	    params: { ... }
206	```
207	
208	Sections `engine`, `correlation`, and `reporting` are optional — omitted keys fall back to the built-in defaults above. Rules are described in [Shipped rules](#shipped-rules-configyaml) and [Adding a new rule](#adding-a-new-rule).
209	
210	Pass `--config PATH` to `analyze` (or `list-reports`) to use a different config file entirely for a single run, instead of editing the bundled `config.yaml`.
211	
212	---
213	
214	## How it works
215	
216	The pipeline is a crash-proof, streaming, single-pass flow:
217	
218	```
219	LogSource(s)  →  parse_file  →  Rule.inspect / flush  →  Correlator  →  AnalysisReport
220	                                                                      ↘ terminal + HTML
221	```
222	
223	### 1. Parsing (`engine/parsers.py`)
224	
225	Every parser implements `LogParser`: a `source` label plus `parse_line(line, line_no) → LogEntry`. Parsers are pure — they raise `MalformedLineError` on bad input and never touch the filesystem themselves.
226	
227	`parse_file(path, parser)` wraps a parser in a crash-proof generator:
228	
229	- Opens with `encoding="utf-8", errors="replace"`.
230	- Skips blank lines.
231	- Yields `LogEntry` on success, or `ParseError` on `MalformedLineError`.
232	- A missing/unreadable file yields a single source-level `ParseError` with `line_no = 0` (callers decide if that is fatal).
233	
234	#### CombinedLogParser (webserver)
235	
236	Parses NCSA Common/Combined access-log lines:
237	
238	```
239	IP identity user [dd/Mon/yyyy:HH:MM:SS +zzzz] "METHOD target proto" status size ["referrer" "user-agent"]
240	```
241	
242	- Referrer/user-agent are optional (Common vs Combined).
243	- Timestamp uses `%d/%b/%Y:%H:%M:%S %z` (timezone-aware).
244	- Produces `WebLogEntry` with `method`, `target` (path **and** query), `status`, etc.
245	- Convenience properties: `path` (no query), `query` (no leading `?`).
246	- A garbage request inside an otherwise valid line is best-effort split (still a signal, not a parse error).
247	
248	#### SyslogAuthParser (auth)
249	
250	Parses BSD syslog:
251	
252	```
253	Mon DD HH:MM:SS host process[pid]: message
254	```
255	
256	BSD syslog has **no year** and **no timezone**. The parser resolves these as follows:
257	
258	- **Year:** pick the year that makes `(month, day, time)` the most recent occurrence at or before `reference_time` (default: now). If the candidate is in the future relative to the reference, subtract one year. An explicit `default_year` can force a fixed year. The CLI supplies `reference_time` automatically (see [Auth-log year anchoring](#auth-log-year-anchoring)).
259	- **Timezone:** attach `tz` (default UTC) so every engine timestamp is tz-aware and comparable with web-log times.
260	
261	Message semantics map to `AuthOutcome`:
262	
263	| Message shape | Outcome |
264	|---|---|
265	| `Failed password for invalid user X from …` | `INVALID_USER` |
266	| `Failed password for X from …` | `FAILURE` |
267	| `Accepted password/publickey for X from …` | `SUCCESS` |
268	| `Connection closed by … [preauth]`, etc. | `OTHER` (IP/port still extracted) |
269	
270	Produces `AuthLogEntry` with `hostname`, `process`, `pid`, `message`, `outcome`, `username`, `source_ip`, `source_port`.
271	
272	---
273	
274	### 2. Detection rules (`engine/rules/`)
275	
276	Every rule implements the same small interface:
277	
278	```python
279	class Rule(ABC):
280	    id: str
281	    severity: Severity
282	
283	    def inspect(self, entry: LogEntry) -> Iterable[Finding]: ...
284	    def flush(self) -> Iterable[Finding]: ...  # end-of-stream aggregates
285	    def reset(self) -> None: ...  # clear state between runs
286	```
287	
288	Rules ignore entry types they don't care about (`isinstance` checks), so the engine feeds **every** entry to **every** rule with no special casing.
289	
290	There are **two algorithm classes**. All shipped detections are instances of one of these — parameters are data, algorithms are code.
291	
292	#### PatternSignatureRule (`type: signature`)
293	
294	Stateless per-line regex matching, aggregated per IP into one `Finding` (emitted on `flush`).
295	
296	| Param | Role |
297	|---|---|
298	| `patterns` | List of regexes |
299	| `target` | Named field extractor (see presets below) |
300	| `case_sensitive` | Default `false` → `re.IGNORECASE` |
301	| `min_hits` | Minimum matches before emit (default 1) |
302	| `max_evidence` | Cap on stored evidence lines |
303	| `max_decode_passes` | Nested URL-decode attempts (default 2) |
304	
305	**Target presets:** `request_target`, `path`, `query`, `user_agent`, `referrer`, `auth_message`.
306	
307	**URL decoding:** matching runs against the union of `{raw, decoded}` forms, with up to 2 recursive `unquote` passes (catches double-encoding like `%252e`). Invalid `%` sequences are left as-is (fail-soft).
308	
309	**Aggregation:** hits for the same IP fold into one finding; `metadata["matches"]` records which pattern/snippet fired. Findings with no IP (e.g. some sudo lines) still aggregate, but the correlator cannot join them across sources.
310	
311	#### ThresholdRule (`type: threshold`)
312	
313	Stateful per-IP sliding window. Fires **one finding per burst** that crosses the threshold.
314	
315	| Param | Role |
316	|---|---|
317	| `match` | Named predicate selecting which events count |
318	| `threshold` | Count that must be reached |
319	| `window_seconds` | Sliding window length |
320	| `distinct_by` | Optional: count distinct field values instead of events |
321	
322	**Match presets:**
323	
324	| Name | Matches |
325	|---|---|
326	| `auth_failure` | Auth `FAILURE` or `INVALID_USER` |
327	| `web_login_failure` | Web 401/403 to a path containing `login` |
328	| `web_404` | Web status 404 |
329	
330	**Distinct-by presets:** `path` (normalized: no query, trailing slash trimmed), `username`.
331	
332	**Burst semantics:**
333	
334	1. On each matching event, append to a per-IP deque.
335	2. Evict events older than `window` relative to the **max timestamp seen for that IP** (tolerates minor out-of-order arrival).
336	3. When count first reaches `threshold`, emit one `Finding`; later events in the same burst update it in place.
337	4. When count drops back below threshold (events age out), the active finding is cleared — a later re-crossing starts a **new** finding.
338	
339	Windows use event timestamps only (never wall-clock / processing time).
340	
341	#### Shipped rules (`config.yaml`)
342	
343	| ID | Type | What it detects | Defaults |
344	|---|---|---|---|
345	| `ssh_brute_force` | threshold | Repeated SSH auth failures from one IP | ≥5 `auth_failure` / 60s → HIGH |
346	| `web_login_brute_force` | threshold | Repeated failed web logins | ≥10 `web_login_failure` / 60s → MEDIUM |
347	| `web_scanning` | threshold | Path enumeration via distinct 404s | ≥15 distinct paths / 120s → MEDIUM |
348	| `directory_traversal` | signature | `../`, `/etc/passwd`, `%2e%2e`, … | any hit → HIGH |
349	| `sql_injection` | signature | `union select`, tautologies, `drop table`, … | any hit → HIGH |
350	| `sensitive_file_exposure` | signature | `.env`, `.git/`, `id_rsa`, `wp-config.php`, … | any hit → HIGH |
351	| `scanner_user_agent` | signature | sqlmap, nikto, nmap, gobuster, … | any hit → MEDIUM |
352	| `sudo_privilege_escalation` | signature | sudo reading shadow/passwd/keys, useradd, … | any hit → CRITICAL |
353	
354	SQL-injection patterns deliberately match SQL *syntax*, never lone metacharacters — a benign `O'Brien` produces zero hits.
355	
356	#### Config → instances
357	
358	```
359	config.yaml  →  load_settings()  →  rule_specs()  →  build_rules()  →  list[Rule]
360	```
361	
362	`build_rules` looks up each `type` in `RULE_TYPES` (populated by `@register`), merges top-level `severity` with `params`, skips `enabled: false`, and instantiates. A later rule with the same `id` overrides an earlier one.
363	
364	---
365	
366	### 3. Correlation (`engine/correlation.py`)
367	
368	After all rules have flushed, `Correlator` groups findings into multi-signal `Incident`s:
369	
370	1. Group findings by `source_ip` (findings with no IP are skipped).
371	2. Sort each IP's findings by `first_seen`.
372	3. Greedily cluster findings whose gap from the running span is ≤ `window` (default **10 minutes**).
373	4. A cluster becomes an incident **only if** it spans ≥2 distinct `rule_id`s **or** ≥2 distinct log sources. A single rule's repeated findings never form an incident — even if far apart.
374	5. Incident severity = one level above the max child severity, capped at CRITICAL.
375	6. `incident_id` is deterministic: `INC-` + `sha1(ip|first_seen|sorted_rule_ids)[:10]`.
376	7. `narrative` summarizes which rules/sources fired and over what span.
377	
378	Correlation is the **only** place cross-source relationships are formed. Stateful rules themselves are single-source (their `match` predicate selects one log type), so the engine does not merge-sort streams across files.
379	
380	**Known limit:** sudo lines often carry no source IP, so `sudo_privilege_escalation` findings cannot be joined into an IP-keyed incident with SSH/web activity from the same attacker.
381	
382	---
383	
384	### 4. Orchestration (`engine/engine.py`)
385	
386	`Engine.analyze(sources) → AnalysisReport` runs the full pipeline:
387	
388	```
389	0. reset() every rule          # safe re-runs on the same Engine instance
390	1. for each LogSource:
391	     parse_file(...)
392	       ParseError  → collect + log warning
393	       LogEntry    → feed to every rule.inspect(); collect eager findings
394	2. flush() every rule          # signature aggregates land here
395	3. cap evidence                # engine-wide max_evidence ceiling
396	4. correlator.correlate(...)   # findings → incidents
397	5. build stats                 # per-source + totals + duration_seconds
398	```
399	
400	**Ordering invariants:**
401	
402	- Sources are consumed **sequentially** (file A fully, then file B) — not merge-sorted by timestamp.
403	- Stateful rules only ever see one source type, so per-file order is enough.
404	- Cross-file relationships are the correlator's job (post-hoc, timestamp-based).
405	
406	**Failure policy:** never crash on bad input. Malformed lines and missing files become `ParseError`s in the report; rule exceptions are logged and skipped.
407	
408	**Report shape:**
409	
410	```python
411	AnalysisReport(
412	    findings: list[Finding],      # per-rule detections
413	    incidents: list[Incident],    # correlated multi-signal groups
414	    parse_errors: list[ParseError],
415	    stats: {
416	        "sources": { "<path>": {lines_read, parsed, malformed, skipped_blank} },
417	        "totals":  { ..., findings, incidents },
418	        "duration_seconds": float,
419	    },
420	)
421	```
422	
423	The CLI then renders the report to the terminal (`cli/render.py`) and persists HTML (`reporter/`).
424	
425	---
426	
427	## File structure
428	
429	```
430	trace-log-sec/
431	├── config.yaml                 # Shipped rules + engine/correlation/reporting (edit this)
432	├── samples/                    # Sample logs with embedded incidents (see incidents_manifest.md)
433	├── src/
434	│   ├── engine/                 # Detection core (format-agnostic)
435	│   │   ├── engine.py           # Orchestrator: parse → detect → correlate
436	│   │   ├── parsers.py          # Combined + syslog parsers, parse_file()
437	│   │   ├── correlation.py      # IP-based finding correlator
438	│   │   └── rules/
439	│   │       ├── base.py         # Rule ABC (inspect / flush / reset)
440	│   │       ├── signature.py    # PatternSignatureRule
441	│   │       ├── threshold.py    # ThresholdRule
442	│   │       ├── registry.py     # @register("type") → RULE_TYPES
443	│   │       ├── factory.py      # build_rules(specs) → Rule instances
444	│   │       └── utils.py        # Shared helpers (presets, evidence)
445	│   ├── models/                 # Dataclasses (parsers, rules, correlation, engine)
446	│   ├── config/
447	│   │   └── settings.py         # YAML → validated settings
448	│   ├── constants/              # Shared literals (windows, formats, defaults)
449	│   ├── cli/                    # Typer CLI
450	│   │   ├── app.py              # Shared Typer app
451	│   │   ├── commands/           # analyze, list-reports
452	│   │   ├── formats.py          # Format sniffing + LogSource construction
453	│   │   ├── validation.py       # Path / .log / uniqueness checks
454	│   │   └── render.py           # Terminal report rendering
455	│   ├── reporter/               # Standalone HTML reports
456	│   │   ├── html.py             # Pure HTML renderer (XSS-safe)
457	│   │   └── storage.py          # write / list / resolve output dir
458	│   ├── utils/                  # Exceptions (MalformedLineError, ConfigError, …)
459	│   └── tests/                  # Unit tests
460	├── docs/                       # Design plans (engine, rules, config)
461	├── task.md                     # Original assignment brief
462	└── pyproject.toml
463	```
464	
465	**Separation of concerns:** the `engine` package is format-agnostic — it accepts structured rule specs (plain dicts), never a YAML path. Config loading lives in `config/`. Format sniffing and presentation (terminal + HTML) live in `cli/` and `reporter/`. Models are split by consumer so each package owns the types it produces.
466	
467	---
468	
469	## Adding a new rule
470	
471	There are three tiers of extensibility. Prefer the cheapest one that fits.
472	
473	### Tier 1 — Retune an existing rule (config only)
474	
475	Edit `config.yaml` (repo root): change `threshold`, `window_seconds`, `severity`, `patterns`, or set `enabled: false`.
476	
477	```yaml
478	- id: ssh_brute_force
479	  type: threshold
480	  severity: critical        # was: high
481	  params:
482	    match: auth_failure
483	    threshold: 3            # was: 5
484	    window_seconds: 30      # was: 60
485	    title: SSH Brute Force
486	```
487	
488	No code changes required.
489	
490	### Tier 2 — New detection using an existing class (config only)
491	
492	Add a new entry with a unique `id` and an existing `type` (`threshold` or `signature`).
493	
494	**Example — credential stuffing** (many distinct usernames failing from one IP):
495	
496	```yaml
497	- id: credential_stuffing
498	  type: threshold
499	  severity: high
500	  params:
501	    match: auth_failure
502	    distinct_by: username
503	    threshold: 20
504	    window_seconds: 300
505	    title: Credential Stuffing
506	    description: Many distinct usernames failing auth from one IP.
507	```
508	
509	**Example — new signature** (XSS probing in the query string):
510	
511	```yaml
512	- id: xss_probe
513	  type: signature
514	  severity: medium
515	  params:
516	    target: query
517	    title: XSS Probe
518	    description: Script-injection syntax in the query string.
519	    patterns:
520	      - "<script\\b"
521	      - "javascript:"
522	      - "onerror\\s*="
523	```
524	
525	Available presets (must already exist in code):
526	
527	| Kind | Names |
528	|---|---|
529	| `match` (threshold) | `auth_failure`, `web_login_failure`, `web_404` |
530	| `distinct_by` (threshold) | `path`, `username` |
531	| `target` (signature) | `request_target`, `path`, `query`, `user_agent`, `referrer`, `auth_message` |
532	
533	If you need a new match predicate or target field, that is Tier 3 (a small code change to the preset dicts in `threshold.py` / `signature.py`) — still cheaper than a whole new algorithm class.
534	
535	### Tier 3 — New algorithm class (code + config)
536	
537	Use this when neither signature nor threshold captures the detection logic (e.g. sequence detection, rate-of-change, cross-field conditions).
538	
539	**Step 1 — Implement the class**
540	
541	Create a module under `src/engine/rules/` (or add to an existing one) and subclass `Rule`:
542	
543	```python
544	# src/engine/rules/sequence.py
545	from __future__ import annotations
546	
547	from collections.abc import Iterable
548	
549	from engine.rules.base import Rule
550	from engine.rules.registry import register
551	from models import Finding, LogEntry, Severity
552	
553	
554	@register("sequence")  # ← makes type: sequence available in config
555	class SequenceRule(Rule):
556	    """Example: fire when event A is followed by event B within a gap."""
557	
558	    def __init__(
559	        self,
560	        *,
561	        id: str,
562	        severity: Severity = Severity.HIGH,
563	        title: str | None = None,
564	        description: str = "",
565	        # …your params…
566	    ) -> None:
567	        self.id = id
568	        self.title = title or id
569	        self.severity = severity
570	        self.description = description
571	        # hold any per-IP state here
572	
573	    def reset(self) -> None:
574	        # clear state so Engine can re-run safely
575	        ...
576	
577	    def inspect(self, entry: LogEntry) -> Iterable[Finding]:
578	        # examine one entry; yield findings eagerly, or return () and
579	        # buffer for flush(). Ignore entry types you don't care about.
580	        ...
581	
582	    def flush(self) -> Iterable[Finding]:
583	        # emit end-of-stream aggregates (like PatternSignatureRule does)
584	        return ()
585	```
586	
587	**Step 2 — Export it**
588	
589	Import the module so `@register` runs at package load. In `src/engine/rules/__init__.py`:
590	
591	```python
592	from engine.rules.sequence import SequenceRule  # noqa: F401  (side-effect: register)
593	
594	__all__ = [..., "SequenceRule"]
595	```
596	
597	Also re-export from `src/engine/__init__.py` if it should be part of the public API.
598	
599	**Step 3 — Wire it in config**
600	
601	```yaml
602	- id: my_sequence_rule
603	  type: sequence
604	  severity: high
605	  params:
606	    title: My Sequence Rule
607	    description: ...
608	    # params map 1:1 to constructor kwargs (except id / severity / type)
609	```
610	
611	**Step 4 — Escape hatch (tests / ad-hoc)**
612	
613	You can also bypass config entirely and pass instances straight to the engine:
614	
615	```python
616	from engine import Engine, SequenceRule
617	from models import Severity
618	
619	engine = Engine(
620	    rules=[
621	        SequenceRule(id="my_sequence_rule", severity=Severity.HIGH, title="…"),
622	    ]
623	)
624	```
625	
626	This is what unit tests typically do.
627	
628	### Checklist for a new rule
629	
630	1. Can you express it with existing `type` + presets? → edit `config.yaml` only.
631	2. Need a new `match` / `target` / `distinct_by` preset? → add a named function to the preset dict in `threshold.py` or `signature.py`, then reference it from config.
632	3. Need a new algorithm? → subclass `Rule`, `@register("name")`, export, add a config entry.
633	4. Add a unit test under `src/tests/test_rules.py` covering the boundary cases (threshold N−1 vs N, pattern hit/miss, flush aggregation, `reset` idempotency).
634	
635	---
636	
637	## Development
638	
639	```bash
640	# Install with test + lint tooling
641	uv sync --group dev --group test
642	
643	# Run the full suite
644	uv run pytest
645	
646	# Lint / format
647	uv run ruff check .
648	uv run ruff format .
649	
650	# Type-check
651	uv run mypy
652	```
653	
654	Sample logs used for end-to-end demos live under `samples/`; see `incidents_manifest.md` there for the embedded attack scenarios.

# trace-log-sec

A security log analysis CLI that parses webserver and authentication logs, detects suspicious activity with configurable rules, and correlates related findings into incidents.

It processes NCSA Combined access logs and BSD syslog auth logs, runs signature and threshold detectors, groups multi-signal activity by IP into correlated incidents, and writes both a terminal summary and a standalone HTML report.

---

## Requirements

- **Python** 3.12 or 3.13
- **[uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/)** (recommended) — installs the project and its dependencies from the lockfile

---

## Installation

Clone the repository and install into a local virtual environment:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Kenndal/trace-log-sec.git
cd trace-log-sec
uv sync
```

That creates `.venv/`, editable-installs the package, and registers the `trace-log-sec` console script.

To include the test tooling as well:

```bash
uv sync --group test
```

For linting / typing / pre-commit hooks:

```bash
uv sync --group dev --group test
```

Verify the install:

```bash
uv run trace-log-sec --help
```

### Alternative: pip

If you prefer pip over uv (still requires Python ≥ 3.12):

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate   # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -e .
trace-log-sec --help
```

---

## CLI usage

The tool exposes two commands: `analyze` and `list-reports`.

```bash
uv run trace-log-sec --help
uv run trace-log-sec analyze --help
uv run trace-log-sec list-reports --help
```

### Analyze logs

```bash
uv run trace-log-sec analyze AUTH.log WEBSERVER.log
```

`analyze` accepts one or more `*.log` files as positional arguments. Format — NCSA Combined access log vs BSD syslog auth log — is **auto-detected per file** from content (first parseable non-blank line within the first 20 lines), so files can be given in any order or mix. The shipped default rule set (`config.yaml` at the repo root) is used, and findings are correlated across files by source IP.

Quick start against the bundled sample logs:

```bash
uv run trace-log-sec analyze \
  samples/auth_incidents.log \
  samples/webserver_incidents.log
```

#### Options

| Option | Overrides | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `--max-evidence N` | `engine.max_evidence` | from `config.yaml` (built-in default: `20`) |
| `--window-minutes N` | `correlation.window_minutes` | from `config.yaml` (built-in default: `10`) |
| `--reference-time DATETIME` | syslog year anchor | newest web-log timestamp in this run, else current UTC time |
| `--config PATH` | the entire config file (rules included) | bundled `config.yaml` at the repo root |

Precedence is always **command-line flag → `config.yaml` → built-in default**: an option only takes effect if explicitly passed.

```bash
uv run trace-log-sec analyze \
  --max-evidence 5 \
  --window-minutes 30 \
  --reference-time 2025-11-12T12:00:00 \
  auth.log webserver.log
```

`--reference-time` accepts `%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S`, `%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S`, or `%Y-%m-%d`.

Use `--config` to swap out the whole config file — rules, `engine`, `correlation`, and `reporting` sections — for a single run, without touching the bundled `config.yaml`:

```bash
uv run trace-log-sec analyze --config custom-config.yaml auth.log webserver.log
```

`--config` must point to an existing, readable file; `--max-evidence`/`--window-minutes` still override whatever that file (or its defaults) sets. `list-reports` also accepts `--config`, so a run's HTML reports can be listed from the same custom `reporting.output_dir`.

#### Input validation

Before analysis starts, every path is checked. Problems are collected and reported together:

- file must exist and be a regular file
- extension must be `.log`
- paths must be unique (duplicates rejected)
- at least one file is required

Unrecognized formats are skipped with a warning (non-fatal), unless *every* given file is unrecognized — that is treated as an error.

#### Auth-log year anchoring

BSD syslog lines have **no year**. The CLI resolves the year as follows:

1. Explicit `--reference-time` if passed
2. Else the newest Combined-log timestamp among web logs in this run (read cheaply from each file’s tail)
3. Else the current UTC time — and a warning is printed, because archived auth-only logs can get the wrong year (which silently skews threshold windows and correlation)

When analyzing both web and auth logs together, you usually do **not** need `--reference-time`. Pass it for historical auth-only runs.

#### Terminal output

```
=== FINDINGS ===
  [HIGH    ] ssh_brute_force        ip=198.51.100.23  count=8   SSH Brute Force
  ...

=== INCIDENTS ===
  INC-a1b2c3d4e5 [HIGH] 203.0.113.150
    ...narrative...

=== PARSE ERRORS ===
  (none)

=== STATS === lines_read=4167 parsed=4160 malformed=7 findings=12 incidents=3 (0.0421s)

HTML report written to reports/report_2026_07_31_12_00_00.html
```

Findings are sorted by severity (highest first), then rule id. Parse errors show source, line number, reason, and a raw snippet.

#### HTML report

Every successful `analyze` also writes a standalone HTML report under the directory configured in `config.yaml` (`reporting.output_dir`, default `reports/`). The directory is created automatically if missing. Filename format:

```
report_YYYY_MM_DD_HH_MM_SS.html
```

Relative paths resolve against the **current working directory**. A write failure (e.g. unwritable directory) only warns — the terminal analysis is never discarded.

The HTML report includes:

- executive summary tiles (findings, incidents, lines read/parsed/malformed, duration)
- correlated incident cards with nested findings and expandable evidence
- findings table (severity, IP, count, sources, time span, description, evidence)
- parse-error table when any malformed lines were seen

All log-derived values are HTML-escaped before embedding (attacker-controlled content must not become stored XSS when the report is opened in a browser).

### List previous reports

```bash
uv run trace-log-sec list-reports
```

Scans `reporting.output_dir` and prints generated reports newest-first with their timestamps. Files that do not match the `report_YYYY_MM_DD_HH_MM_SS.html` naming convention are ignored. A missing directory yields an empty result, not an error.

Accepts `--config PATH` as well, to list reports from a custom config's `reporting.output_dir` instead of the bundled `config.yaml`'s.

## Configuration

All runtime knobs live in `config.yaml` at the repo root (shipped with the package):

```yaml
engine:
  max_evidence: 20          # ceiling on evidence lines stored per finding

correlation:
  window_minutes: 10        # IP clustering window for incidents

reporting:
  output_dir: reports       # HTML report directory (cwd-relative or absolute)

rules:
  - id: ssh_brute_force
    type: threshold
    severity: high
    params: { ... }
```

Sections `engine`, `correlation`, and `reporting` are optional — omitted keys fall back to the built-in defaults above. Rules are described in [Shipped rules](#shipped-rules-configyaml) and [Adding a new rule](#adding-a-new-rule).

Pass `--config PATH` to `analyze` (or `list-reports`) to use a different config file entirely for a single run, instead of editing the bundled `config.yaml`.

---

## How it works

The pipeline is a crash-proof, streaming, single-pass flow:

```
LogSource(s)  →  parse_file  →  Rule.inspect / flush  →  Correlator  →  AnalysisReport
                                                                      ↘ terminal + HTML
```

### 1. Parsing (`engine/parsers.py`)

Every parser implements `LogParser`: a `source` label plus `parse_line(line, line_no) → LogEntry`. Parsers are pure — they raise `MalformedLineError` on bad input and never touch the filesystem themselves.

`parse_file(path, parser)` wraps a parser in a crash-proof generator:

- Opens with `encoding="utf-8", errors="replace"`.
- Skips blank lines.
- Yields `LogEntry` on success, or `ParseError` on `MalformedLineError`.
- A missing/unreadable file yields a single source-level `ParseError` with `line_no = 0` (callers decide if that is fatal).

#### CombinedLogParser (webserver)

Parses NCSA Common/Combined access-log lines:

```
IP identity user [dd/Mon/yyyy:HH:MM:SS +zzzz] "METHOD target proto" status size ["referrer" "user-agent"]
```

- Referrer/user-agent are optional (Common vs Combined).
- Timestamp uses `%d/%b/%Y:%H:%M:%S %z` (timezone-aware).
- Produces `WebLogEntry` with `method`, `target` (path **and** query), `status`, etc.
- Convenience properties: `path` (no query), `query` (no leading `?`).
- A garbage request inside an otherwise valid line is best-effort split (still a signal, not a parse error).

#### SyslogAuthParser (auth)

Parses BSD syslog:

```
Mon DD HH:MM:SS host process[pid]: message
```

BSD syslog has **no year** and **no timezone**. The parser resolves these as follows:

- **Year:** pick the year that makes `(month, day, time)` the most recent occurrence at or before `reference_time` (default: now). If the candidate is in the future relative to the reference, subtract one year. An explicit `default_year` can force a fixed year. The CLI supplies `reference_time` automatically (see [Auth-log year anchoring](#auth-log-year-anchoring)).
- **Timezone:** attach `tz` (default UTC) so every engine timestamp is tz-aware and comparable with web-log times.

Message semantics map to `AuthOutcome`:

| Message shape | Outcome |
|---|---|
| `Failed password for invalid user X from …` | `INVALID_USER` |
| `Failed password for X from …` | `FAILURE` |
| `Accepted password/publickey for X from …` | `SUCCESS` |
| `Connection closed by … [preauth]`, etc. | `OTHER` (IP/port still extracted) |

Produces `AuthLogEntry` with `hostname`, `process`, `pid`, `message`, `outcome`, `username`, `source_ip`, `source_port`.

---

### 2. Detection rules (`engine/rules/`)

Every rule implements the same small interface:

```python
class Rule(ABC):
    id: str
    severity: Severity

    def inspect(self, entry: LogEntry) -> Iterable[Finding]: ...
    def flush(self) -> Iterable[Finding]: ...  # end-of-stream aggregates
    def reset(self) -> None: ...  # clear state between runs
```

Rules ignore entry types they don't care about (`isinstance` checks), so the engine feeds **every** entry to **every** rule with no special casing.

There are **two algorithm classes**. All shipped detections are instances of one of these — parameters are data, algorithms are code.

#### PatternSignatureRule (`type: signature`)

Stateless per-line regex matching, aggregated per IP into one `Finding` (emitted on `flush`).

| Param | Role |
|---|---|
| `patterns` | List of regexes |
| `target` | Named field extractor (see presets below) |
| `case_sensitive` | Default `false` → `re.IGNORECASE` |
| `min_hits` | Minimum matches before emit (default 1) |
| `max_evidence` | Cap on stored evidence lines |
| `max_decode_passes` | Nested URL-decode attempts (default 2) |

**Target presets:** `request_target`, `path`, `query`, `user_agent`, `referrer`, `auth_message`.

**URL decoding:** matching runs against the union of `{raw, decoded}` forms, with up to 2 recursive `unquote` passes (catches double-encoding like `%252e`). Invalid `%` sequences are left as-is (fail-soft).

**Aggregation:** hits for the same IP fold into one finding; `metadata["matches"]` records which pattern/snippet fired. Findings with no IP (e.g. some sudo lines) still aggregate, but the correlator cannot join them across sources.

#### ThresholdRule (`type: threshold`)

Stateful per-IP sliding window. Fires **one finding per burst** that crosses the threshold.

| Param | Role |
|---|---|
| `match` | Named predicate selecting which events count |
| `threshold` | Count that must be reached |
| `window_seconds` | Sliding window length |
| `distinct_by` | Optional: count distinct field values instead of events |

**Match presets:**

| Name | Matches |
|---|---|
| `auth_failure` | Auth `FAILURE` or `INVALID_USER` |
| `web_login_failure` | Web 401/403 to a path containing `login` |
| `web_404` | Web status 404 |

**Distinct-by presets:** `path` (normalized: no query, trailing slash trimmed), `username`.

**Burst semantics:**

1. On each matching event, append to a per-IP deque.
2. Evict events older than `window` relative to the **max timestamp seen for that IP** (tolerates minor out-of-order arrival).
3. When count first reaches `threshold`, emit one `Finding`; later events in the same burst update it in place.
4. When count drops back below threshold (events age out), the active finding is cleared — a later re-crossing starts a **new** finding.

Windows use event timestamps only (never wall-clock / processing time).

#### Shipped rules (`config.yaml`)

| ID | Type | What it detects | Defaults |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ssh_brute_force` | threshold | Repeated SSH auth failures from one IP | ≥5 `auth_failure` / 60s → HIGH |
| `web_login_brute_force` | threshold | Repeated failed web logins | ≥10 `web_login_failure` / 60s → MEDIUM |
| `web_scanning` | threshold | Path enumeration via distinct 404s | ≥15 distinct paths / 120s → MEDIUM |
| `directory_traversal` | signature | `../`, `/etc/passwd`, `%2e%2e`, … | any hit → HIGH |
| `sql_injection` | signature | `union select`, tautologies, `drop table`, … | any hit → HIGH |
| `sensitive_file_exposure` | signature | `.env`, `.git/`, `id_rsa`, `wp-config.php`, … | any hit → HIGH |
| `scanner_user_agent` | signature | sqlmap, nikto, nmap, gobuster, … | any hit → MEDIUM |
| `sudo_privilege_escalation` | signature | sudo reading shadow/passwd/keys, useradd, … | any hit → CRITICAL |

SQL-injection patterns deliberately match SQL *syntax*, never lone metacharacters — a benign `O'Brien` produces zero hits.

#### Config → instances

```
config.yaml  →  load_settings()  →  rule_specs()  →  build_rules()  →  list[Rule]
```

`build_rules` looks up each `type` in `RULE_TYPES` (populated by `@register`), merges top-level `severity` with `params`, skips `enabled: false`, and instantiates. A later rule with the same `id` overrides an earlier one.

---

### 3. Correlation (`engine/correlation.py`)

After all rules have flushed, `Correlator` groups findings into multi-signal `Incident`s:

1. Group findings by `source_ip` (findings with no IP are skipped).
2. Sort each IP's findings by `first_seen`.
3. Greedily cluster findings whose gap from the running span is ≤ `window` (default **10 minutes**).
4. A cluster becomes an incident **only if** it spans ≥2 distinct `rule_id`s **or** ≥2 distinct log sources. A single rule's repeated findings never form an incident — even if far apart.
5. Incident severity = one level above the max child severity, capped at CRITICAL.
6. `incident_id` is deterministic: `INC-` + `sha1(ip|first_seen|sorted_rule_ids)[:10]`.
7. `narrative` summarizes which rules/sources fired and over what span.

Correlation is the **only** place cross-source relationships are formed. Stateful rules themselves are single-source (their `match` predicate selects one log type), so the engine does not merge-sort streams across files.

**Known limit:** sudo lines often carry no source IP, so `sudo_privilege_escalation` findings cannot be joined into an IP-keyed incident with SSH/web activity from the same attacker.

---

### 4. Orchestration (`engine/engine.py`)

`Engine.analyze(sources) → AnalysisReport` runs the full pipeline:

```
0. reset() every rule          # safe re-runs on the same Engine instance
1. for each LogSource:
     parse_file(...)
       ParseError  → collect + log warning
       LogEntry    → feed to every rule.inspect(); collect eager findings
2. flush() every rule          # signature aggregates land here
3. cap evidence                # engine-wide max_evidence ceiling
4. correlator.correlate(...)   # findings → incidents
5. build stats                 # per-source + totals + duration_seconds
```

**Ordering invariants:**

- Sources are consumed **sequentially** (file A fully, then file B) — not merge-sorted by timestamp.
- Stateful rules only ever see one source type, so per-file order is enough.
- Cross-file relationships are the correlator's job (post-hoc, timestamp-based).

**Failure policy:** never crash on bad input. Malformed lines and missing files become `ParseError`s in the report; rule exceptions are logged and skipped.

**Report shape:**

```python
AnalysisReport(
    findings: list[Finding],      # per-rule detections
    incidents: list[Incident],    # correlated multi-signal groups
    parse_errors: list[ParseError],
    stats: {
        "sources": { "<path>": {lines_read, parsed, malformed, skipped_blank} },
        "totals":  { ..., findings, incidents },
        "duration_seconds": float,
    },
)
```

The CLI then renders the report to the terminal (`cli/render.py`) and persists HTML (`reporter/`).

## File structure

```
trace-log-sec/
├── config.yaml                 # Shipped rules + engine/correlation/reporting (edit this)
├── samples/                    # Sample logs with embedded incidents (see incidents_manifest.md)
├── src/
│   ├── engine/                 # Detection core (format-agnostic)

│   │   ├── parsers.py          # Combined + syslog parsers, parse_file()
│   │   ├── correlation.py      # IP-based finding correlator
│   │   └── rules/

│   │       ├── signature.py    # PatternSignatureRule
│   │       ├── threshold.py    # ThresholdRule

│   │       ├── factory.py      # build_rules(specs) → Rule instances
```

**Separation of concerns:** the `engine` package is format-agnostic — it accepts structured rule specs (plain dicts), never a YAML path. Config loading lives in `config/`. Format sniffing and presentation (terminal + HTML) live in `cli/` and `reporter/`. Models are split by consumer so each package owns the types it produces.

---

## Adding a new rule

There are three tiers of extensibility. Prefer the cheapest one that fits.

### Tier 1 — Retune an existing rule (config only)

Edit `config.yaml` (repo root): change `threshold`, `window_seconds`, `severity`, `patterns`, or set `enabled: false`.

```yaml
- id: ssh_brute_force
  type: threshold
  severity: critical        # was: high
  params:
    match: auth_failure
    threshold: 3            # was: 5
    window_seconds: 30      # was: 60
    title: SSH Brute Force
```

No code changes required.

### Tier 2 — New detection using an existing class (config only)

Add a new entry with a unique `id` and an existing `type` (`threshold` or `signature`).

**Example — credential stuffing** (many distinct usernames failing from one IP):

```yaml
- id: credential_stuffing
  type: threshold
  severity: high
  params:
    match: auth_failure
    distinct_by: username
    threshold: 20
    window_seconds: 300
    title: Credential Stuffing
    description: Many distinct usernames failing auth from one IP.
```

**Example — new signature** (XSS probing in the query string):

```yaml
- id: xss_probe
  type: signature
  severity: medium
  params:
    target: query
    title: XSS Probe
    description: Script-injection syntax in the query string.
    patterns:
      - "<script\\b"
      - "javascript:"
      - "onerror\\s*="
```

Available presets (must already exist in code):

| Kind | Names |
|---|---|
| `match` (threshold) | `auth_failure`, `web_login_failure`, `web_404` |
| `distinct_by` (threshold) | `path`, `username` |
| `target` (signature) | `request_target`, `path`, `query`, `user_agent`, `referrer`, `auth_message` |

If you need a new match predicate or target field, that is Tier 3 (a small code change to the preset dicts in `threshold.py` / `signature.py`) — still cheaper than a whole new algorithm class.

### Tier 3 — New algorithm class (code + config)

Use this when neither signature nor threshold captures the detection logic (e.g. sequence detection, rate-of-change, cross-field conditions).

**Step 1 — Implement the class**

Create a module under `src/engine/rules/` (or add to an existing one) and subclass `Rule`:

```python
# src/engine/rules/sequence.py
from __future__ import annotations

from collections.abc import Iterable

from engine.rules.base import Rule
from engine.rules.registry import register
from models import Finding, LogEntry, Severity


@register("sequence")  # ← makes type: sequence available in config
class SequenceRule(Rule):
    """Example: fire when event A is followed by event B within a gap."""

    def __init__(
        self,
        *,
        id: str,
        severity: Severity = Severity.HIGH,
        title: str | None = None,
        description: str = "",
        # …your params…
    ) -> None:
        self.id = id
        self.title = title or id
        self.severity = severity
        self.description = description
        # hold any per-IP state here

    def reset(self) -> None:
        # clear state so Engine can re-run safely
        ...

    def inspect(self, entry: LogEntry) -> Iterable[Finding]:
        # examine one entry; yield findings eagerly, or return () and
        # buffer for flush(). Ignore entry types you don't care about.
        ...

    def flush(self) -> Iterable[Finding]:
        # emit end-of-stream aggregates (like PatternSignatureRule does)
        return ()
```

**Step 2 — Export it**

Import the module so `@register` runs at package load. In `src/engine/rules/__init__.py`:

```python
from engine.rules.sequence import SequenceRule  # noqa: F401  (side-effect: register)

__all__ = [..., "SequenceRule"]
```

Also re-export from `src/engine/__init__.py` if it should be part of the public API.

**Step 3 — Wire it in config**

```yaml
- id: my_sequence_rule
  type: sequence
  severity: high
  params:
    title: My Sequence Rule
    description: ...
    # params map 1:1 to constructor kwargs (except id / severity / type)
```

**Step 4 — Escape hatch (tests / ad-hoc)**

You can also bypass config entirely and pass instances straight to the engine:

```python
from engine import Engine, SequenceRule
from models import Severity

engine = Engine(
    rules=[
        SequenceRule(id="my_sequence_rule", severity=Severity.HIGH, title="…"),
    ]
)
```

This is what unit tests typically do.

### Checklist for a new rule

1. Can you express it with existing `type` + presets? → edit `config.yaml` only.
2. Need a new `match` / `target` / `distinct_by` preset? → add a named function to the preset dict in `threshold.py` or `signature.py`, then reference it from config.
3. Need a new algorithm? → subclass `Rule`, `@register("name")`, export, add a config entry.
4. Add a unit test under `src/tests/test_rules.py` covering the boundary cases (threshold N−1 vs N, pattern hit/miss, flush aggregation, `reset` idempotency).

    DEFAULT_CORRELATION_WINDOW_MINUTES,

    id: str
    type: str
    enabled: bool = True

    """Top-level ``Engine`` behavior, independent of any single rule."""

    max_evidence: int = DEFAULT_MAX_EVIDENCE


class CorrelationConfig(BaseModel):
    """``Correlator`` behavior: how findings are clustered into incidents."""

    window_minutes: float = DEFAULT_CORRELATION_WINDOW_MINUTES


class ReportingConfig(BaseModel):
    """HTML report output behavior (see :mod:`reporter`)."""

    output_dir: str = DEFAULT_REPORTS_DIR

    rules: list[RuleSpec]
    engine: EngineConfig = Field(default_factory=EngineConfig)
    correlation: CorrelationConfig = Field(default_factory=CorrelationConfig)
    reporting: ReportingConfig = Field(default_factory=ReportingConfig)


def load_settings(path: str | Path = DEFAULT_CONFIG_PATH) -> EngineSettings:
    """Read and validate the YAML config at ``path``.

    Raises ``ConfigError`` (never a raw ``OSError``/``yaml.YAMLError``/
    ``pydantic.ValidationError``) so callers get one consistent, informative
    failure type for every way a hand-authored config file can be broken.
    """
    try:
        with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
            data = yaml.safe_load(f)
    except OSError as e:
        raise ConfigError(path, str(e)) from e
    except yaml.YAMLError as e:
        raise ConfigError(path, f"malformed YAML: {e}") from e

    try:
        return EngineSettings.model_validate(data)
    except ValidationError as e:
        raise ConfigError(path, str(e)) from e

    """Convert validated rule specs into the plain dicts ``build_rules`` expects.

    A later rule with the same ``id`` overrides an earlier one (per the
    ``config.yaml`` header comment), keeping the first-seen position.
    """
    by_id: dict[str, dict[str, Any]] = {}
    for r in settings.rules:
        by_id[r.id] = r.model_dump(exclude_none=True)
    return list(by_id.values())

"""Every custom exception raised by this project, kept in one place.

Modules that need one of these import it from here rather than defining
their own local exception class, so the full set of project-specific error
types has a single, obvious home.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from pathlib import Path


class TraceLogSecError(Exception):
    """Base class for every custom exception raised by this project."""


class ConfigError(TraceLogSecError):
    """Raised when the YAML config at a given path can't be read or is invalid."""

    def __init__(self, path: str | Path, reason: str) -> None:
        self.path = path
        self.reason = reason
        super().__init__(f"invalid config at {path!r}: {reason}")


class MalformedLineError(TraceLogSecError):
    """Raised by a parser when a line cannot be parsed."""

    def __init__(self, reason: str) -> None:
        super().__init__(reason)
        self.reason = reason


class RuleConfigError(TraceLogSecError):
    """Raised when a rule spec, constructor argument, or preset name is invalid."""


class CliInputError(TraceLogSecError):
    """Raised when CLI-supplied arguments (e.g. log file paths) fail validation."""

    def __init__(self, reason: str) -> None:
        self.reason = reason
        super().__init__(reason)


class ReportError(TraceLogSecError):
    """Raised when an HTML report can't be written to disk.

    Wraps the underlying ``OSError`` (e.g. permission denied, unwritable
    output directory) so callers get one consistent, informative failure type
    — mirroring how ``ConfigError`` normalizes config-load failures.
    """

    def __init__(self, path: str | Path, reason: str) -> None:
        self.path = path
        self.reason = reason
        super().__init__(f"could not write report to {path!r}: {reason}")

        load_settings(f)

### What happens on missing / invalid / malformed config

- Missing/unreadable file → `OSError` caught → `ConfigError(path, str(e))`.
- Malformed YAML syntax → `yaml.YAMLError` caught → `ConfigError(path, "malformed YAML: …")`.
- Schema-invalid data (missing required key, wrong types, non-mapping top level, empty file → `None`) → Pydantic `ValidationError` caught → `ConfigError(path, str(e))`.

Missing keys within optional sections just fall back to their model defaults (`Field(default_factory=...)` on `EngineSettings`, lines 54–58). An omitted `engine`/`correlation`/`reporting` section is fully defaulted; an omitted `rules` key is a validation error (it is required).

Documented `analyze` options: `--max-evidence N` (overrides `engine.max_evidence`), `--window-minutes N` (overrides `correlation.window_minutes`), `--reference-time DATETIME` (syslog year anchor; accepts `%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S`, `%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S`, or `%Y-%m-%d`), `--config PATH` (swap whole config file). Precedence: command-line flag → `config.yaml` → built-in default.

Documented features: per-file auto-detection of log format (from first parseable non-blank line within first 20 lines); input validation (must exist, be a regular file, `.log` extension, unique paths, at least one file; unrecognized formats skipped with a warning unless all are unrecognized); auth-log year anchoring (explicit `--reference-time` → newest web-log timestamp → current UTC with warning); crash-proof streaming single-pass pipeline (parse → rule inspect/flush → correlate → report); terminal output with FINDINGS/INCIDENTS/PARSE ERRORS/STATS sections; standalone XSS-safe HTML report named `report_YYYY_MM_DD_HH_MM_SS.html`; correlation logic (group by source_ip, greedy cluster within window, incident only if ≥2 rule_ids or ≥2 sources, deterministic `INC-<sha1>` ids); two rule algorithm classes (`PatternSignatureRule`, `ThresholdRule`) with named presets; a three-tier extensibility guide for adding rules; and a full `File structure` section. It also documents known limits (sudo lines carry no IP; SQLi patterns match syntax not lone metacharacters).
